clue.text: Man, perhaps going by car, left city

parts.note: taken as written
the Isle of Man is an example of an island, so 'Man, perhaps' stands for isle

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a city by car, perhaps heading for the ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but it is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, so 'Man, perhaps' is any isle. CARLISLE is a city in northern England near the Scottish border.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle is a cathedral city in Cumbria, England, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Plant tea down in front of someone who plays …

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed in front of another sits above it, so this word comes first

parts.note: char is informal British slang for a cup of tea
the ellipsis runs on into the next clue's game, rugby, where a lock is a second-row forward

explanation.surface: Gardening notes: put the tea down in front of a player, a sentence left trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The '…' carries the clue on into 2 Down, whose 'This game' is rugby, so the player is a LOCK, a second-row forward. CHAR is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlock is wild mustard, a yellow-flowered weed of fields, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: … This game (good in red)

indicators.note: the clue puts the letter for good inside the gemstone word for red

parts.note: ruby is a deep red colour, named after the gemstone

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, a game played well by a side in red.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues 1 Down through the '…', and 'This game' is the definition: rugby is the game a lock plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a ball sport, and 'this game' points to the sport the previous clue's player belongs to.

clue.text: Street worker goes under home for a brief moment

indicators.note: in a down clue the pieces after this phrase are written beneath the word for home

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a worker ant is the classic crossword worker

explanation.surface: A street worker heads home, gone in a flash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is the crossword's usual ANT, after the worker caste of an ant colony.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant is a split second, the shortest span of time.

clue.text: Garlands worn by notable islanders

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the phrase that follows, as if being worn by it

explanation.surface: Famous islanders put on garlands of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'notabLE ISlanders'. Hawaiian islanders, the clue's picture, really do wear such garlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Leis are Hawaiian garlands of flowers worn round the neck.

clue.text: Record established by American in field event

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A new record is set by an American athlete in a field event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' reads as an athletic best, but it is a gramophone DISC.
explanation.definitionFit: The discus throw is an athletics competition held on the field rather than the track.

clue.text: Come into home — the woman's the bee's knees!

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
her is the possessive for a woman
the bee's knees means the very best thing, and slang 'it' means the same, as in 'she thinks she's it'

explanation.surface: Arriving home, someone declares that the woman is simply the best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bee's knees' is old slang for the finest thing, and so is IT, as in 'you are it'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into money or property is to receive it as a bequest when someone dies.

clue.text: Plots against dreamers in Oxford

parts.note: con is used for against, as in pros and cons
the poet Matthew Arnold called Oxford the city of dreaming spires, so the dreamers there are its towers

explanation.surface: A group of idle dreamers at Oxford University hatch plots against someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dreamers' are not students but the spires, from Matthew Arnold's description of Oxford as 'that sweet city with her dreaming spires'.
explanation.definitionFit: To conspire is to scheme secretly together, so a verb meaning schemes.

clue.text: What could produce second church with distinctive doctrine

definitions.text: What could produce second church with distinctive doctrine

parts.note: an ism is any distinctive doctrine or theory

explanation.surface: Asking what event might give rise to a breakaway church with its own beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a split in a church yields a second church with its own beliefs.
explanation.definitionFit: A schism is a split within a religious body, which can leave a rival breakaway church.

clue.text: Saint in east appearing at end of month

indicators.note: the pieces given before this phrase are written at the end of the month word

parts.note: August is the eighth month

explanation.surface: A saint shows up in the east at the close of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: IN is taken as written and E is east; both follow the month word.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustine of Hippo, and Augustine of Canterbury, are both canonised figures of the early Church.

clue.text: Six seen in garden prior to church confirmation?

indicators.note: in this down clue the garden group comes before, so above, the church letters
the Roman numeral for six is seen inside the name of the garden

parts.note: Eden is the Biblical Garden of Eden
VI is six in Roman numerals
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Six people are spotted in a garden before church, ahead of a confirmation service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confirmation' suggests the church rite, but here it means proof; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence is proof that backs up a claim, as confirmation does.

clue.text: Vague idea held by Hamish, unchallenged

indicators.note: the letters are held inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Hamish holds on to a vague notion that nobody bothers to dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'HamisH, UNCHallenged'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunch is an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on firm facts.

clue.text: Song by head of music, an amateur practitioner

parts.note: a lay is an old word for a song or ballad

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A song by the head of the music department, who turns out to be merely an amateur.
explanation.walkthrough: LAY is a poetic word for a song or ballad, as in 'The Lay of the Last Minstrel'.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman is a non-professional, someone without expert training in a field.

clue.text: Interrupts sir heartlessly with stupid rioting outside

indicators.note: the rearranged letters of the word stupid go round the trimmed sir
rioting suggests wild disorder, so the letters of stupid are rearranged
heartless means the middle letter of the word sir is removed

explanation.surface: Someone cuts in on a gentleman while foolish rioters rage outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interrupts' could pass for part of the wordplay, but it is the definition; 'rioting' gives DIUPTS, which 'outside' wraps round the heartless sir.
explanation.definitionFit: To disrupt is to break into or upset an ongoing activity, much as interrupting does.

clue.text: Interrogation in which it's impossible to keep cool?

definitions.text: Interrogation in which it's impossible to keep cool?

parts.words: Interrogation in which it's impossible to keep cool?
parts.note: a fierce questioning makes the subject sweat, and the word for it also names cooking under intense heat, where nothing stays cool

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the questioning; the cryptic twist is that the same word means cooking under a hot element, where nothing could stay cool.
explanation.definitionFit: A grilling is an intense session of questioning, named after cooking over fierce heat.

clue.text: I create fortune dodgily, bringing out a naughty moneymaker

indicators.note: dodgily suggests something done crookedly, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the letter removed from the pool

explanation.surface: A crook boasts of making a fortune by shady means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgily' rearranges ICREATEFORTUNE and 'bringing out' takes away the A, leaving the thirteen letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A forger of banknotes makes money illegally, so a naughty moneymaker in a punning sense.

clue.text: A Parisian spring with man free to go anywhere

parts.note: un is French for a, as a Parisian would say it
a bound is a leap or spring
Ed is a man's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A Frenchman leaps along with a companion, at liberty to roam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Parisian' means 'a' in French, UN; ED is a common short form of the name Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbounded means having no limits, so no restriction on movement.

clue.text: Royalty may be so enormous

definitions.meaning: royals may behave like the son of a monarch, as befits a prince
lavish or very large, as in a handsome sum of money

explanation.surface: Royals might be very large indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Princely describes behaviour fit for a monarch's son, and also a lavish amount, as in a princely sum.

clue.text: Warship is something that hurts cows, Spooner says

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two pieces trade their first letters

parts.note: cows are cattle
a bruiser is something, or someone, that inflicts bruises

explanation.surface: A warship described as something that harms livestock, says the famous word-muddler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cattle bruiser' with the first sounds swapped becomes the name of a heavily armed warship.
explanation.definitionFit: A battlecruiser was a large, fast, heavily gunned naval vessel of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Eat nuts going bad, resulting in infection

indicators.note: going bad suggests decay, so the letters of eat nuts are scrambled

explanation.surface: Eating rotten nuts leads to an infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going bad' rearranges the letters of 'Eat nuts'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tetanus is a bacterial disease, often from wounds, so it is an infection.

clue.text: Nation with wet weather to the east, not our country

parts.note: for a British newspaper, our country is the UK
rain is wet weather

explanation.surface: Describing a nation with rain blowing in from the east, and insisting it is not Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Telegraph is British, so 'our country' is the UK; the 'not' is the joke, since the nation built from it is a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukraine is a sovereign state in eastern Europe.

clue.text: A very loud tune engenders concern

parts.note: FF stands for fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud
an air is a melody or tune

explanation.surface: A very loud piece of music causes worry.
explanation.walkthrough: FF is the musical marking fortissimo, 'very loud'.
explanation.definitionFit: An affair is a matter or business that concerns someone, as in 'that's my affair'.

clue.text: Spurt gets female to Everest, maybe, not male

indicators.note: not here means the letter for male is left out of the peak

parts.note: Everest is an example of a mountain

explanation.surface: A woman makes a dash towards Everest, though no man joins her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurt' is a noun here, a jet of water; 'not male' drops a letter from the peak, and the female letter goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A fountain is a jet or spurt of water forced into the air.

clue.text: Harp on about child in unfortunate situation

indicators.note: about here means the letters of harp on are moved around

explanation.surface: Going on and on about a child in a sad plight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' rearranges the letters of 'Harp on'.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphan is a youngster whose parents have died, a sadly unlucky position.

clue.text: Make out time from ticker

parts.note: to make out sounds is to hear them

explanation.surface: Trying to make out the time from a clock's ticking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ticker' suggests a clock, but it is slang for the organ that beats in the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticker is informal slang for the organ that pumps blood, from its beat.

clue.text: Old ship's load beginning to fall off

indicators.note: the start of the word for load drops away, so its first letter is removed

parts.note: a cargo is a load carried by a ship

explanation.surface: An old ship's load starts to topple overboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' looks like the word to take a first letter from, but 'beginning to fall off' says the start of CARGO goes, leaving the four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the vessel of Jason and the Argonauts in Greek myth.

clue.text: A fellow pocketing old penny as extra charge

indicators.note: the fellow puts the penny in his pocket, so it goes inside his letters

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
D was the abbreviation for a penny in British money before 1971

explanation.surface: A man slips an old coin into his pocket as a surcharge.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for a penny in pre-decimal British currency (from the Latin denarius); a DON is a college fellow at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: An add-on is a supplement, something tacked on at further cost.

clue.text: I greet man casually as 'bud'

indicators.note: casually suggests a loose, careless arrangement, so the letters of I greet man are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone greets a man informally, calling him 'bud'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bud' looks like the American 'buddy', which the casual greeting supports, but it is the verb to sprout.
explanation.definitionFit: To bud is to sprout new growth, as a seed does when it starts to grow.

clue.text: Bit of food in kitchen vessel given to artist

indicators.note: the vessel is handed to the artist, so its letters follow his

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's usual artist
a dish is a kitchen vessel

explanation.surface: A morsel of food in a kitchen bowl is handed to a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A radish is a small salad root vegetable, a small item to eat.

clue.text: Rope always attached to wood

indicators.note: the word for always is fixed onto the end of the wood

parts.note: a forest is a large wood
ay is an old or poetic word for always, also spelt aye

explanation.surface: A rope is permanently tied to a piece of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: AY (or AYE) is an archaic word for 'ever, always'.
explanation.definitionFit: A forestay is a rigging line running from a mast to the bow of a boat.
